content: Nebulin-related-anchoring protein (N-RAP) is a protein encoded by the NRAP gene in humans. It is a muscle-specific isoform that belongs to the nebulin family of proteins. This family consists of five members: N-RAP, nebulin, nebulette, LASP-1, and LASP-2. N-RAP plays a role in myofibrillar myogenesis during development and in maintaining cell-cell connections in mature muscle tissue. Structure N-RAP is a protein with a molecular weight of 197 kDa and is composed of 1730 amino acids. As a member of the nebulin family, it is characterized by 35 amino acid stretches known as nebulin repeats, which are actin-binding domains containing a conserved SDxxYK motif. Similar to nebulin, groups of seven single repeats within N-RAP form super repeats, which include a conserved WLKIGW motif at the end of the third repeat. A distinguishing feature of N-RAP, compared to nebulin, is its N-terminal cysteine-rich LIM domain, a characteristic it shares with LASP-1 and LASP-2. Function N-RAP has a critical role in the organization of myofibrils during cardiomyocyte development. It is essential for the proper α-actinin-dependent organization of myofibrils in cardiomyocytes. Studies have shown that reducing N-RAP protein levels leads to the disassembly of myofibrils in embryonic cardiomyocytes. Specifically, N-RAP super repeats are thought to serve as a scaffold for organizing α-actinin and actin into sarcomeric I-Z-I complexes in premyofibrils. Dynamic imaging studies have demonstrated that N-RAP departs from the I-Z-I complexes once actin thin filament assembly is complete. In adult cardiac muscle, N-RAP is localized to intercalated discs, where it anchors terminal actin filaments to the sarcolemma. It has been suggested that in mature muscle, N-RAP plays a role in force transduction from the sarcomere to the extracellular matrix. Clinical Significance Although no direct link has been established between N-RAP mutations and human cardiomyopathies, N-RAP has been found to be significantly upregulated in murine models of dilated cardiomyopathy. This upregulation is hypothesized to be an adaptive response aimed at correcting disorganized actin thin filament architecture at intercalated disc junctions in cardiomyocytes during dilated cardiomyopathy.
